refs.quote: Dopamine is a natural catecholamine formed by the decarboxylation of 3,4-dihydroxyphenylalanine (DOPA). It is a precursor to norepinephrine in noradrenergic nerves and is also a neurotransmitter in certain areas of the central nervous system, especially in the nigrostriatal tract, and in a few peripheral sympathetic nerves.

mechanism_of_action.value: Endogenous catecholamine acting on dopaminergic (D1/D2), beta-1 adrenergic (inotropic/chronotropic at 5-10 mcg/kg/min), and alpha-1 adrenergic (vasoconstriction >10 mcg/kg/min) receptors.

value.management: Reduce recommended starting dosage of dopamine to no greater than one-tenth (1/10) of the usual dose.

tier.note: 5-axis synthesis: No human pregnancy data; norepinephrine is preferred in maternal shock because dopamine carries higher arrhythmia risk and potential uterine vasoconstriction.

refs.quote: There are no human data with dopamine use in pregnant women. There are risks to the mother and fetus from hypotension associated with shock, which can be fatal if left untreated ( see Clinical Considerations ).

pregnancy_pk.value: No pregnancy PK adjustment established; reserve for select bradycardic shock where norepinephrine is unsuitable, with fetal monitoring.

refs.quote: There are risks to the mother and fetus from hypotension associated with shock, which can be fatal if left untreated ( see Clinical Considerations ).

postpartum.value: Standard ICU weaning applies postpartum; note that dopamine suppresses maternal prolactin and may inhibit lactation initiation.

refs.quote: However, dopamine is a physiological prolactin-inhibiting factor that suppresses maternal serum prolactin secretion and can inhibit lactogenesis or reduce breastmilk production during infusion.

lactation_rid.value: Not established (poor oral absorption; suppresses maternal prolactin)

refs.quote: No data are available on the excretion of dopamine into human milk. Dopamine has poor oral bioavailability and a plasma half-life of approximately 2 minutes. Summary of Use during Lactation: Intravenous dopamine is not expected to be absorbed orally by a breastfed infant.

lactation_summary.value: Oral infant absorption is negligible, but intravenous dopamine suppresses maternal prolactin and can inhibit milk production during infusion; production recovers after stopping.

refs.quote: There are no data regarding the presence of dopamine in human milk, the effects of dopamine on the breastfed infant, or the effects of the drug on milk production. 8.4 Pediatric Use Dopamine HCl infusions have been used in pediatric patients from birth through adolescence.
However, dopamine is a physiological prolactin-inhibiting factor that suppresses maternal serum prolactin secretion and can inhibit lactogenesis or reduce breastmilk production during infusion.

value.diluent: Compatible with D5W or 0.9% NaCl (avoid alkaline solutions such as sodium bicarbonate); e.g., 200 mg/50 mL (4,000 mcg/mL) syringe or 400 mg/250 mL (1,600 mcg/mL).
value.rate: 2 to 5 mcg/kg/min initial; titrate in 5-10 mcg/kg/min increments (max 50 mcg/kg/min).
value.instructions: Infuse into a large central vein via calibrated infusion pump; avoid extravasation (phentolamine rescue if extravasation occurs).

refs.quote: Administer Dopamine HCl in Dextrose Injection into a large vein [see Warnings and Precautions (5.1) ] with the use of an infusion pump preferably in an intensive care setting. Remove outer wrap (moisture and oxygen barrier) only when ready to administer the product. Discard product if outer wrap is damaged (e.g., tears or holes).
